newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Exit poll shows Bulgaria's Stoyanov elected.
newsitem.headline: Exit poll shows Bulgaria's Stoyanov elected.

text.p: First indications from Bulgaria's presidential election run-off on Sunday showed voters had handed a decisive victory to opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov over his rival from the ex-communist ruling party.
A telephone exit poll by the independent Fakt agency gave reformist lawyer Stoyanov 63 percent to 37 percent for Socialist Culture Minister Ivan Marazov.

The poll of 1,060 voters across the country was broadcast by private Darik radio. MBMD polling agency said it expected a similarly wide gap from its projections based on actual voting figures but had no details yet.
"There is a trend for a big difference between the two candidates," said MBMD head Mira Yanova.

Supporters of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) were already celebrating in some parts of Sofia before the official close of polls at 7 p.m (1700 GMT). "It's a triumph," said Georgi Gechev, 35.
The central Electoral Commission said about 50 percent of the electorate had voted by 4 p.m. (1400 GMT), slightly more than last week's first round turnout.
Although the president has limited powers under Bulgaria's post-communist constitution, a big win for Stoyanov could severely weaken the Socialist government of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov.
Even workers in the smokestack industries of Bulgaria's red heartland said they had deserted the Socialists, who won a majority in parliamentary elections in December 1994.

Seven years after overthrowing their communist rulers, Bulgarians are still waiting for the benefits promised from democracy and a market economy and now face a winter of food and fuel shortages harking back to communist rule.
Bombings and other violence have marred Bulgaria's second post-communist presidential campaign, culminating in the murder last month of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.

Shortly after Sunday's voting began, a caller telephoned a bomb threat to a city centre school where President Zhelyu Zhelev was due to cast his ballot. A thorough search found nothing, state radio said.
Zhelev, a pro-market liberal like Stoyanov, lost a U.S.-style primary in June and has not stood for re-election.
Stoyanov won 43.9 percent in the first round last weekend, comfortably ahead of Marazov but short of the 50 percent he needed to win outright.
The run-off coincides with an International Monetary Fund mission discussing terms for release of a delayed $115 million credit vital to stop Bulgaria defaulting on its foreign debt.
Stoyanov and his UDF accuse the government of moving too slowly to privatise state firms and close big loss-makers.
Bulgaria has managed to privatise a mere five percent of state industry, with most of the cash going into the pockets of shadowy business groupings close to the Socialists.

Neighbouring Romania and Yugoslavia, also voting on Sunday, are themselves battling economic crisis but Bulgaria has the lowest foreign investment in the region and a quarter of its numerous banks are in receivership.
